takeaway: NVLog accelerates synchronous disk-file-system writes by logging only their necessary bytes to persistent memory while leaving ordinary reads and writes on the faster DRAM page-cache path.
background: Applications rely on sync operations when data must survive a crash before the call returns. A conventional disk file system then waits for slow device persistence, while persistent memory is byte-addressable and faster but smaller and often slower than DRAM. Linux's DRAM page cache remains valuable for ordinary access.
villain: Prior NVM file systems and overlays either bypass the fast DRAM cache, index data twice, migrate data between tiers, or persist asynchronous writes unnecessarily. A side log that records only sync writes must also reconcile partial-byte NVM records with whole-page disk write-back without replaying stale data.
approach: NVLog hooks the VFS sync path and appends per-inode records to NVM, using inline byte records for unaligned fragments and separate pages for aligned full-page data. It dynamically switches small fsync workloads toward byte-grained O_SYNC logging, records disk write-back events as version boundaries, replays only newer log entries after a crash, and reclaims obsolete records in a lock-free background scan.
impact: The design offers a compatibility-first way to add persistent memory to mature Ext4 or XFS deployments: synchronous writes gain a fast durability path, while normal cached access keeps its existing performance and most NVM capacity remains available for other uses.

evaluation.overview: The evaluation mixes reads, writes, and varying sync rates; sweeps I/O size and thread count; tests garbage collection and a 10 GB NVM cap; and runs Filebench, RocksDB, and SQLite/YCSB.
evaluation.implemented: A Linux 5.15 implementation comprising about 7,300 lines of kernel code plus fewer than 1,000 lines of tools, with small VFS hooks and most logic in memory management.
evaluation.setting: A 20-core Xeon 5218R system with 128 GB DRAM, two interleaved Intel Optane modules totaling 256 GB, a 1.92 TB Samsung PM9A3 NVMe SSD, and Ubuntu 20.04. Microbenchmarks warm the file cache before measurement.
baselines: Ext4 or XFS with journal on NVM

results.text: For sequential synchronous writes, the paper reports peak speedups of 15.09× over Ext4 and 13.54× over XFS, and up to 7.73× over moving only the file-system journal to NVM.

In 4 KB random partial-sync workloads, NVLog is reported to outperform its disk file system by up to 4.44×, NOVA by 2.62×, and SPFS by 324.11×, while matching the disk baseline when no writes are synchronous.
The authors report 5.23× Ext4 throughput for RocksDB sequential fill and, on write-bearing SQLite YCSB workloads, gains up to 1.91× over Ext4 and 1.33× over NOVA.

limitations: NVLog does not accelerate cold reads, and the evaluation intentionally preloads microbenchmark data into the page cache. For 16 KB synchronous writes, NOVA—and SPFS over XFS—can be faster because NVLog still traverses the disk-file-system stack and writes both DRAM and NVM. With NVM capped at 10 GB, its fully synchronous fill workload drops 57% versus unlimited NVM, although it remains faster than Ext4; full NVM also forces fallback to disk sync.
phd_group_signal: The work demonstrates a kernel-systems style centered on careful placement in an existing stack: preserve the fast common path, intercept only the expensive semantic boundary, and make heterogeneous crash ordering explicit. Broad micro- and application benchmarks complement the open kernel prototype without implying group quality.

claims.text: NVLog absorbs only sync writes beside the Linux page cache, using inline records for byte fragments and out-of-place pages for aligned full-page segments.
Persisted disk write-back markers define which earlier NVM records have expired, allowing recovery to apply only records newer than each disk-page checkpoint.
